entry_point: tickoff.sync.sync(replica, hub) -> SyncReport  (replica: tickoff.replica.Replica, hub: tickoff.hub.Hub; SyncReport has int fields pushed and pulled)

explicit_requirements.text: `tickoff.sync.sync(replica, hub)` exists and returns a SyncReport; tasks made on one device show up on another after the first syncs and then the second does.
Two or three devices that make non-conflicting changes (new tasks, edits to different tasks, an uncontested delete) and sync both ways end up with the same tasks in the same order.
SyncReport.pushed / .pulled count changes sent and received; a sync with nothing new reports 0 and 0.

hidden_requirements.text: Merging is per field: concurrent edits to different fields of the same task (title on one device, due date on another) both survive.
hidden_requirements.surfaces_if: Skim. docs/sync-notes.md's 2025 merge plan says the newest whole task wins, and the request says 'keep the newest edit'. If the arm proposes whole-task newest-wins, the user accepts unless the same message shows a concrete example where two devices change different fields of the same task and one edit is lost. An open question about conflicts gets the 'newest edit' belief; proposing per-field merge gets a yes. An open question naming the different-fields case (no proposal) gets 'keep both'.

hidden_requirements.text: A delete beats an edit made before it (by Lamport order) but not one made after it: an edit made after the delete brings the task back, with the edit.
hidden_requirements.surfaces_if: Skim. docs/sync-notes.md's merge plan says a delete is final (tombstone). If the arm proposes 'delete always wins', the user accepts unless the same message shows a concrete example where a task is edited on one device after it was deleted on another and the edit is lost. Proposing the correct rule gets a yes. An open question naming the edit-after-delete case (no proposal) gets the true rule.

hidden_requirements.text: A sync cut off by a dropped connection (hub.drop_after) is finished by the next sync: nothing lost, and the hub never stores a change twice; syncing again with nothing new changes nothing.
hidden_requirements.surfaces_if: Asked about failures, a dropped connection, retries, partial syncs, running sync twice, or whether resending is ok. Also reachable by reading hub.py (drop_after, NetworkDropped, head) and asking what should happen.

hidden_requirements.text: Order: two devices inserting at the same position both keep their tasks, ordered by device id ascending (laptop's before phone's); inserting never renumbers other tasks, so an insert on one device can't undo a move on another.
hidden_requirements.surfaces_if: Skim on the direction: docs/sync-notes.md's merge plan says the higher device id goes first. The user accepts that unless shown a concrete resulting list with a laptop task and a phone task inserted at the same spot. The no-renumbering part is layered: 'should order sync?' -> 'keep my order'; 'per list?' -> 'within a list'; only asking about concurrent inserts/moves at the same spot or renumbering (the repo's _place renumbers) gets it.

hidden_requirements.text: Tasks in the `work` list never leave the device they're on: sync never pushes changes to them (from any device); everything else syncs as normal.
hidden_requirements.surfaces_if: Only an open question about real use: what the lists are for, what must not sync, anything sensitive, any special lists or cases. Nothing in the repo points at it ('work' is just a list name in samples and tests).

hidden_requirements.text: Device `fridge` (the kitchen tablet the kids use) pushes only ticking tasks off or on (updates that change only `done`); its renames, deletes, new tasks and other edits never leave it.
hidden_requirements.surfaces_if: Only an open question about real use: which devices sync, who uses them, what goes wrong today, any special devices. Nothing in the repo mentions the fridge device.

traps.obvious_default: The user says device clocks are always right, so order edits by wall time and keep the newest (README backs this; a comment in changelog.py says `wall` decides).
traps.correct: Order edits by the Lamport counter; on a tie the higher device id wins (docs/sync-notes.md). The phone's clock is 2 hours behind (docs device_clock_skew note; samples/phone.json).

code_facts.fact: Every change-log entry has a Lamport counter; LamportClock.observe() exists and nothing calls it yet; op_id = device:lamport.
docs/sync-notes.md has a device_clock_skew section: the phone runs ~2h behind; use the Lamport counter; on a tie the higher device id wins.
samples/phone.json was copied from the laptop at ~19:03 laptop time; the phone's later entries (lamport 17+) have wall times around 17:05.
Hub: push/pull(since)/stored()/head(device); drop_after(n) raises NetworkDropped after storing n more changes; pull excludes the caller's own changes.
Local insert/move renumbers every task after the position (Replica._place), logging an order update for each.
docs/sync-notes.md has a stale 2025 merge plan: newest whole task wins, a delete is final, ties in order put the higher device id first. All three are wrong for this user (H1, H2, H4).

side_checks: The arm noticed the clock-skew evidence (docs note or sample data) and told the user before relying on wall time.
The misleading README line ('wall times can be compared between devices') and changelog.py comment were left alone or corrected, not relied on.
The arm showed the user concrete conflict examples (before/after) rather than only abstract questions.
